Nov 3 (Reuters) - US crude oil and gasoline inventories were expected to have risen last week, while distillate stockpiles likely declined, an extended Reuters poll showed on Tuesday.

Eight analysts polled by Reuters estimated, on average, that crude inventories rose by about 880,000 barrels in the week ended October 30.

Crude inventories fell by 1.9 million barrels to 410.6 million barrels in the week ended October 23, the EIA said, compared with analysts' expectations in a Reuters poll for a 15,000-barrel rise.

PHOENIX, Tuesday, November 03 2026 - Ahead of this morning's market opening, Southern Copper Corporation closed lower the previous trading day. Southern Copper Corporation (NYSE:SCCO), the NYSE's largest Non ferrous metals sector company by market cap, fell 2.2% during its previous trading session to close at $173.49.

Southern Copper Corporation (NYSE:SCCO) is a leading integrated copper producer, renowned for its extensive copper mining operations and low-cost production capabilities. Core activities encompass large-scale copper mining, smelting, and refining through key assets like the Toquepala and Cuajone mines, alongside Mexico's strategic copper operations. The company excels in producing copper concentrates and cathodes, while also generating molybdenum and silver byproducts. Southern Copper sustains its competitive edge through significant copper reserves, supporting industrial copper supply and expansion projects. Emphasizing sustainability, the company adopts innovative mining practices and maintains robust supply chain management, positioning itself to leverage long-term trends in electric vehicles and base metals demand.

NYSE STOCK REPORT

PHOENIX, Tuesday, November 03 2026 - Ahead of this morning's market opening, Southern Copper Corporation closed lower the previous trading day. Southern Copper Corporation (NYSE:SCCO), the NYSE's largest Non ferrous metals sector company by market cap, fell 2.2% during its previous trading session to close at $173.49.

Southern Copper Corporation (NYSE:SCCO) is a leading integrated copper producer, renowned for its extensive copper mining operations and low-cost production capabilities. Core activities encompass large-scale copper mining, smelting, and refining through key assets like the Toquepala and Cuajone mines, alongside Mexico's strategic copper operations. The company excels in producing copper concentrates and cathodes, while also generating molybdenum and silver byproducts. Southern Copper sustains its competitive edge through significant copper reserves, supporting industrial copper supply and expansion projects. Emphasizing sustainability, the company adopts innovative mining practices and maintains robust supply chain management, positioning itself to leverage long-term trends in electric vehicles and base metals demand.

Southern Copper Corporation (NYSE:SCCO) is a leading integrated copper producer, renowned for its extensive copper mining operations and low-cost production capabilities. Core activities encompass large-scale copper mining, smelting, and refining through key assets like the Toquepala and Cuajone mines, alongside Mexico's strategic copper operations. The company excels in producing copper concentrates and cathodes, while also generating molybdenum and silver byproducts. Southern Copper sustains its competitive edge through significant copper reserves, supporting industrial copper supply and expansion projects. Emphasizing sustainability, the company adopts innovative mining practices and maintains robust supply chain management, positioning itself to leverage long-term trends in electric vehicles and base metals demand.

Company Profile

Southern Copper Corporation is an integrated copper producer operating mining units and metallurgical facilities in Mexico and Peru, with exploration activities in Argentina, Chile, Mexico and Peru. It is 88.9% owned by Grupo Mexico and listed in New York and Lima. Net sales reached $13,237.0 million in the first nine months of 2026, up 38.6% year over year, driven by higher prices across all products and modestly higher zinc sales volumes, partly offset by lower copper, molybdenum and silver volumes. Copper remains the principal revenue source, supplemented by molybdenum, zinc and silver by-products. Refined copper and rod output rose 10.1% year to date, while mined copper fell 2.9% on lower Peruvian ore grades.

CIUDAD DE MÉXICO, 4 nov (Reuters) - Analistas de grupos financieros y corredurías opinan sobre los mercados mexicanos y la economía. A continuación, un resumen de los reportes del 4 de noviembre. Las opiniones reflejadas no representan puntos de vista de Reuters.

PEPPERSTONE - Los mercados reevalúan las perspectivas políticas y económicas de Estados Unidos tras el control demócrata del Congreso. La renta variable cayó con fuerza al inicio de la sesión, especialmente el sector tecnológico, aunque los principales índices recuperaban terreno mientras los inversionistas evaluaban un Gobierno dividido.

* El peso mexicano MXN= se apreciaba un 0.9%, a 18.6505 unidades por dólar, frente a las 18.8208 unidades del precio de referencia de LSEG del martes.

BANORTE - Prevemos que la recuperación continúe. Una ruptura por debajo de 18.60 establecería una señal favorable. La siguiente resistencia se ubica en 18.50, mientras que el soporte está en 18.77. Recomendamos mantener posiciones.

ING - Los sondeos de opinión acertaron y los demócratas lograron una contundente victoria en las elecciones legislativas de Estados Unidos. Las tasas de interés de corto plazo estadounidenses y el dólar bajan ligeramente, mientras que los futuros accionarios recuperan parte de las pérdidas de entre 2% y 3% registradas durante la noche.

* El principal índice de la bolsa mexicana, el S&P/BMV IPC .MXX, subió el martes un 0.58%, a 70,184.33 puntos.

COPKAPITAL - El índice inició el mes con fuerza y alcanzó en las primeras horas un máximo intradía de 71,337.85 puntos, con un avance del 2.2%. Posteriormente moderó sus ganancias, aunque mantuvo como soporte el nivel psicológico de 70,000 puntos.

GBM - Los futuros estadounidenses apuntan al alza tras recuperarse de las fuertes pérdidas iniciales, provocadas por la contundente victoria demócrata en las elecciones legislativas.

(Reporte de Noé Torres)

(( noe.torres@thomsonreuters.com ;))

The Weekly Consumer Price Index (IPC-S) decelerated in the seven capitals surveyed at the end of October, according to the Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV). The index rose by 0.32%, a result lower than the previous report of 0.46%, during the transition from the third to the fourth four-week period of the month.

The most significant deceleration among the capitals occurred in Recife (from 0.92% to 0.79%) and São Paulo (from 0.52% to 0.37%).

Following these are Belo Horizonte (from 0.49% to 0.34%), Salvador (from 0.38% to 0.33%), Rio de Janeiro (from 0.65% to 0.26%), Brasília (from 0.37% to 0.24%), and Porto Alegre (from 0.16% to 0.12%).

Exports of goods from Latin America and the Caribbean outpaced the global average in the first half of the year, with Mexico leading the way due to increased sales of equipment for artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure in the United States, as highlighted by the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB).

Shipments from the region rose 19.5 percent annually in the first semester, surpassing the 14.5 percent growth in global trade. "The main driver was the volume, with Mexico at the forefront for its AI equipment, while higher mining and energy prices supported sales from South America and the Caribbean," the report stated.

In its Trade and Integration Monitor report published yesterday, the IDB detailed that Mexico's foreign trade grew by 24.6 percent in the first half of the year, driven by an increase in manufacturing purchases from the United States, primarily for information processing equipment, servers, and electronic components for building data centers and AI infrastructure in that country.

Such was the demand from this industry that it accounts for the entirety of Mexico's growth in 2025 and between 75 and 80 percent of the growth recorded in the first half of 2026, according to IDB estimates.

Regionally, these goods for computing infrastructure boosted export growth, but in Latin America and the Caribbean, the advancement "almost entirely depends on one country."

In this context, it points out that Mexico accounts for 93 percent of regional exports of data processing equipment, servers, and electronic components for building data centers, as well as 96 percent of the increase recorded last year.

The report provides insights into the region's participation in various segments of the AI-related value chain. "Final equipment – computers, servers, and communication devices – accounted for 60.4 percent of regional exports, but when excluding Mexico, this proportion falls to 9.9 percent, while intermediate inputs explain 81.7 percent. This means that while Mexico exports finished products, the rest of the region contributes with parts and components in limited amounts," it elaborated.

In terms of foreign direct investment, the IDB notes that regarding investment from China, Mexico's share of the flow towards the region increased from 4.3 percent in 2023 to 44.2 percent by 2025, with operations concentrated in manufacturing, the primary sector, and electricity generation.

For months, the world has been waiting for the U.S. legislative elections to see if the conflict in the Middle East can finally be resolved. With Iran previously refusing to negotiate, using the opportunity to politically harm Donald Trump in the elections through high oil prices, the situation is shifting with this Democratic victory that opens up new scenarios.

One possibility is that the American president resumes military actions as a tool to force an agreement favorable to U.S. interests, even if that leads to another spike in oil prices.

"The biggest risk of new military actions is in the week following the elections. However, reaching an agreement is unlikely, as the positions of the United States and Iran remain far apart. Therefore, the possibility of maintaining the current status quo is real. Trump could maintain the blockade and attempt to economically pressure Iran, a strategy that requires time and patience. In the face of this outcome, it is unclear whether Trump has that time," said Sebastián Borgarello, VP & Global Head of Energy Consulting at S&P Global.

The U.S. Energy Information Administration adds to this scenario with projections of $105 per barrel for crude oil in the last quarter of the year, dropping only by the end of 2027 to $74.

This outlook is similar to that of Goldman Sachs and HSBC, which do not expect the market to stabilize until mid-2027. "With failed diplomacy and flows yet to recover, Brent could reach $120 per barrel before easing in the third quarter of 2027," explained the consulting firm Economía & Energía regarding the perspective of the Chinese bank.

In this context, Álvaro Ríos Rocca, Director of Gas Energy Latin America, opined that due to damage to refineries caused by the war, which will take one to three years to resolve, and a broken trust between the United States and Iran, "crude will continue to be priced between $90 and $100 in the next twelve months."

Conversely, the more optimistic view suggests that, whether due to pressure from major multinationals, Trump's weakening in the wake of the elections, or aligning interests with China, which is also heavily impacted by this dispute, prices might begin to decline with the eventual normalization of transit through the Strait of Hormuz.

This perspective is supported by Citi Bank, which considers the blockade in Hormuz unsustainable and expects a reopening before the end of the year that would increase crude oil supply by 3 to 4 million barrels per day. In this way, the price would finish the year at $70 and average $65 in 2027.

"In reasonable terms, both the United States and Europe will likely want to increase their oil reserves, which are at historic lows. This will lead to the lifting of sanctions on Russia to bring more crude to the market. The big risk is that in a potential impeachment scenario, Trump may respond with increased military action. A wartime president always has more tools to thwart an impeachment," emphasized Gustavo Pérego, director of the consulting firm ABECEB.

Under this blue wave scenario, international analyst Miguel Ponce stated, "if Trump assumes he is a lame duck and does not disregard Congress, large companies will demand that he end the war as soon as possible. However, in my opinion, this will not be resolved until the meeting with Xi Jinping and Putin scheduled for November is finalized."

What would be the best scenario for Argentina?

The 54% increase in exports leaves no room for doubt. This year, Argentina's energy trade surplus increased by more than $4 billion compared to 2025, a 75% jump attributed to both higher volumes and elevated prices.

In addition to the good news for public finances, local oil companies' revenue surged by over $5.1 billion, according to a report from Economía & Energía. This figure is crucial for isolating the sector from the local economic crisis, as a high country risk would otherwise hinder financing for many projects.

However, the flip side of rising exports is an increase in energy costs that impacts the economy both through reduced disposable income for families and industrial competitiveness.

Moreover, the fuel market is at a critical juncture with a significant price gap relative to international levels due to the buffer launched by YPF. The most affected players are the refineries, which report a nearly 30% delay in diesel pump prices.

"The best future scenario would be a normalization of the international conflict, but with prices sustained at a level higher than before the war, around $85 or $90 per barrel," stated a major local Oil & Gas firm.

Certificates of Deposit (CDTs) in Colombia may begin to offer lower yields in the coming months, depending on market expectations regarding the decisions of the Banco de la República.

For now, the Issuer's decision to maintain the interest rate at 12.25% will allow these products to retain their current yields in the coming weeks, with offers reaching up to 13.1% annual effective rate for one-year investments, according to the fintech MejorCDT.

The company explained that the rates for these savings instruments are typically related to the behavior of the reference rate set by the Banco de la República. Therefore, keeping it at the current level helps banks continue to offer high yields in the short term.

However, the outlook could change if financial entities begin to anticipate a reduction in interest rates. In that scenario, initial adjustments may focus on CDTs with longer terms, even before the Issuer officially announces a reduction.

The intervention rate increased from 9.25% to 12.25% during 2026, following several increases. The most recent decision to maintain it at that level did not receive unanimous support from the Board of Directors: four members voted in favor of keeping it, while three opposed.

This division keeps the discussion about the direction of monetary policy open for the remainder of the year. The next meeting of the Board of Directors, where the interest rate will be reviewed again, is scheduled for December 18.

What will happen to those who already have a CDT?

An eventual reduction in yields does not mean that savers who have already contracted these products will receive less money than agreed. The rate of a CDT is set at the time of investment and remains unchanged for the agreed term.

Omar Casas, General Manager of MejorCDT, explained that the uncertainty regarding the upcoming decisions of the Banco de la República does not alter the conditions of the deposits that are already in effect.

"When the Board of the Banco de la República splits on a vote, no one can be sure of what will happen in December. Savers should not carry that uncertainty; when opening a CDT, they know from day one how much they will earn, and that amount is guaranteed until maturity, regardless of whether rates go up or down thereafter," he stated.

Therefore, any potential changes would primarily affect the conditions of new investments, as banks would have the ability to modify the rates offered to those who decide to open a CDT after those adjustments.

Inflation and savings: the outlook for CDTs in Colombia

Another factor influencing the performance of these products is inflation. In September, the annual variation of the consumer price index reached 6.29%, the highest since July 2024 and a figure that remains above the 3% target set by the Banco de la República.

Meanwhile, core inflation, which excludes food and regulated prices, fell from 6.1% to 6.0% during the same period.

In this context, Casas noted that the rates available in the market allow for returns that exceed the annual increase in prices.

"Currently, the bank's rate outpaces inflation by nearly 6 percentage points. This means that well-placed money not only withstands the cost of living but also gains ground," he remarked.

Savings figures also show a shift in Colombians' preferences. The balances of individuals in CDTs reached $158 trillion, while deposits in savings accounts totaled $127 trillion.

The difference between the two products is $31 trillion, a gap that, according to MejorCDT, had not been recorded before 2023. For the fintech, this behavior reflects savers' interest in alternatives that offer a defined yield from the moment of contracting.

In this context, the company believes that there are still opportunities for those looking to invest their resources through these instruments, although it warns that current rates could change according to monetary policy decisions and the expectations of financial entities.

"It is still possible to find CDTs with very competitive yields today, but that window will not be open forever," Casas cautioned.

The archive of LA PATRIA preserves encounters with Antonio Navarro Wolff that allow us to remember some of the reflections he shared about Colombia, its political history, and the pursuit of peace.

The former commander of the M-19, who passed away in Bogotá last Sunday (November 1), spoke with this newspaper in 2005 and participated in a meeting with students in Manizales in 2016. Although these were different settings, he addressed issues related to the armed conflict and the country's future on both occasions.

His Presidential Aspirations and the Quest for Peace

On October 9, 2005, LA PATRIA published an interview conducted by Álvaro Segura López, then Opinion Editor, during Navarro Wolff's visit to Manizales.

At that time, the political leader was campaigning for the presidential candidacy of the left, amid discussions to unite the Polo Democrático Independiente and Alternativa Democrática ahead of the 2006 elections.

During the conversation, he spoke about his aspirations, the political situation in the country, and the strategies of Álvaro Uribe's government regarding the armed conflict.

One of the topics he addressed was presidential re-election. Navarro expressed his agreement with this concept, but not immediately, as he believed it could permit abuses of power.

"I agree that the figure of re-election should exist, but not immediately because it allows the one in power to abuse it," he stated.

He also commented on the humanitarian exchange between the government and the FARC. In his view, both parties were politically exploiting the issue and were not treating it with the humanitarian approach it required.

"The humanitarian agreement has had very little that is humanitarian; neither the FARC nor the government has treated it that way; they have handled it politically and militarily," he asserted.

In the interview, he also shared his vision for resolving the armed conflict. He believed that efforts should not focus solely on the confrontation between the government and the guerrillas but must also include the rural population.

"Every additional dollar, every additional peso that needs to be invested to seek solutions to the conflict, I would invest in rural development, in social development, and in winning over the rural population in the conflict areas," he stated.

During that visit to Manizales, he also outlined his programmatic proposals, which he grouped into three priorities: education, employment, and social justice; peace; and the fight against corruption.

Remembering History to Avoid Repeating Mistakes

The second account occurred on May 31, 2016, when Navarro Wolff participated in the National Youth Political Forum, organized by San Rafael School in Manizales.

On that occasion, the then-senator of the Alianza Verde engaged with students about the history of violence in Colombia and the importance of understanding past events.

His remarks began with an invitation for the youth to learn history to prevent the repetition of the mistakes that have marked the country.

During the meeting, he recalled the assassination of Jorge Eliécer Gaitán in 1948 and the violence between liberals and conservatives. He also spoke about the emergence of peasant guerrillas and his own involvement in the M-19.

LA PATRIA's publication reminded readers that Navarro had attempted to negotiate with the state in 1985, but withdrew from the process after a grenade was thrown at him in Cali.

Referring to the peace process that was ongoing in Colombia at the time, he expressed confidence that an agreement would be signed that year. However, he also voiced concern about the polarization surrounding the negotiations.

By Gabriel Burin

BUENOS AIRES, Nov 4 (Reuters) - The outlook for Brazil's currency has weakened on policy doubts following the re-election of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, a Reuters poll of foreign exchange strategists showed.

Market players worry Lula may fail to deliver sufficient fiscal adjustment to tackle Brazil's chronic budget issues compounded by spending promises during the election campaign.

The real BRL=, BRBY closed on Tuesday at its weakest level since December, extending losses to more than 9% after Lula's victory in the October 25 second-round vote. But year-to-date, the currency is virtually flat.

In 12 months, it is seen at 5.37 per dollar or 2.6% softer than the 5.23 expected for the same period one month ago, though 2.2% stronger than Tuesday's close, according to the median estimate of 23 FX strategists polled from October 30 to November 3.

Answers to an extra question reflected the most pessimistic sentiment towards the currency in the survey's recent history.

Twelve of 13 respondents said the risks to their forecasts were tilted to the downside. One said "neutral" and none said the risks were tilted toward appreciation.

"Recent statements by the re-elected president suggest public spending will rise over the next four years," said Marcela Kawauti, chief economist at Lifetime Investimentos, referring to Lula's campaign promises.

"This expansionary fiscal stance is likely to push up country risk, putting significant pressure on the currency and leading to a depreciation of the real."

A report saying Lula could meet an influential economist who has proposed slashing Brazil's benchmark interest rate, which at 13.75% is one of the highest among the world's biggest economies, further unnerved investors. The country's finance minister denied such a proposal was on the table.

The real's downtrend may be stemmed somewhat if Lula signals fiscal moderation before starting his next term in January, analysts said. A possible central bank decision to hold rates later on Wednesday would also help the currency.

Over the medium term, the complicated domestic outlook may combine with less favorable external conditions to add pressure on Brazil's currency.

Santander economists wrote that a persistent drop in crude oil prices could hurt the real as Brazil is a net exporter.

"Second...a surprise extra (interest rate) cut here in Brazil or surprise extra hike in the US would compress the differential, reduce carry and also provide weaker support for the currency."

(Other stories from the November Reuters foreign exchange poll)

PHOENIX, Tuesday, November 03 2026 - Ahead of this morning's market opening, Southern Copper Corporation closed lower the previous trading day. Southern Copper Corporation (NYSE:SCCO), the NYSE's largest Non ferrous metals sector company by market cap, fell 2.2% during its previous trading session to close at $173.49.

Southern Copper Corporation (NYSE:SCCO) is a leading integrated copper producer, renowned for its extensive copper mining operations and low-cost production capabilities. Core activities encompass large-scale copper mining, smelting, and refining through key assets like the Toquepala and Cuajone mines, alongside Mexico's strategic copper operations. The company excels in producing copper concentrates and cathodes, while also generating molybdenum and silver byproducts. Southern Copper sustains its competitive edge through significant copper reserves, supporting industrial copper supply and expansion projects. Emphasizing sustainability, the company adopts innovative mining practices and maintains robust supply chain management, positioning itself to leverage long-term trends in electric vehicles and base metals demand.

MBJ Airports Limited, the operator of Sangster International Airport in Montego Bay, St James, is advising the public that it will conduct a full-scale emergency simulation exercise at the facility on Wednesday, November 4.

The exercise, dubbed Exercise Red Falcon, is scheduled to begin at 7:00 a.m. and last approximately two hours.

MBJ says the simulation will involve an aircraft safety incident and require a coordinated response from its Emergency Response Services and its mutual aid partners, including the Jamaica Fire Brigade, the Jamaica Constabulary Force, the Jamaica Defence Force and the Ministry of Health and Wellness.

The airport says the exercise is being conducted in keeping with the requirements of the Jamaica Civil Aviation Authority and the International Civil Aviation Organization, which mandate a full-scale emergency exercise every two years.

The airport's last full-scale emergency exercise was held in October 2024.

The exercise will assess all aspects of MBJ's Emergency Response Plan and test the effectiveness of coordination between the airport and the country's principal first-response agencies.

"Authoritarianism simply attracts people who cannot tolerate complexity; there is nothing intrinsically leftist or rightist about this instinct."

Anne Applebaum, The Twilight of Democracy

I hear many comments labeling Donald Trump as a right-wing or extreme right President. However, the Peterson Institute for International Economics published an article in September by Collen S. Hendrix pointing out that "government control of the U.S. economy, or socialism, has expanded dramatically in 2025 under a Republican White House and Congress."

Most of this deterioration has been a result of government acquisition of shares, not through expropriations or nationalizations, but that does not erase the intensity of the trend. "Under Trump's government, the United States has acquired a portfolio of shares or equity-like instruments in over 30 firms in the semiconductor, critical minerals, and quantum computing sectors, with the most significant acquisition being a 10% stake in Intel negotiated in 2025," wrote Hendrix.

The article only assesses government ownership of companies, but Trump's economic interventionism has been more notable in foreign trade. Traditionally, Republicans defended free trade. Ronald Reagan correctly asserted that tariffs are taxes paid by consumers. George H.W. Bush also pushed for free trade when he negotiated the North American Free Trade Agreement. In contrast, Democrats, usually more nationalist and protectionist, demanded the imposition of tariffs on imports.

Trump has discarded free trade and imposed tariffs on all kinds of products, even those that the trade agreement with Mexico exempts. Like the mercantilists of the 19th century and the socialists of the 20th, he has claimed that this protectionism will generate a renaissance of industrial activity in the country, but the only result has been rising prices to the irritation of consumers and voters.

Trump's immigration policies, including raids, have also been contrary to those of previous Republican presidents. This November 6 marks the 40th anniversary of the immigration amnesty declared by Reagan in 1986, which granted permanent residency and a legal path to citizenship to 3 million immigrants, many of them Mexican, who had lived in the United States uninterrupted since 1982.

Trump has adopted other policies characteristic of socialist or authoritarian regimes. His rejection of press freedom, for example, has led to his inclusion in the list of "Press Freedom Predators 2026" by Reporters Without Borders. Trump has declared that a free press is the number one public enemy of the American Union.

Left or right labels have been surpassed by reality. Today, we have a few liberal governments in the world that respect individual freedoms, including economic ones, and many authoritarian ones, whether left or right. Trump has never been liberal; he is simply authoritarian, but in economic matters, he leans towards socialism.

Nationality

It appears that Beatriz Gutiérrez Müller has indeed started the process to obtain Spanish nationality. According to The Objective, the application was accepted on April 30, 2025. AMLO's wife reportedly received preferential treatment.

Since Javier Milei and Donald Trump strengthened their political ties, the relationship between Argentina and the United States has begun to translate into an increasingly broad economic agenda. The alignment between the two leaders has resulted in trade agreements, financial negotiations, and investment projects in strategic sectors.

This relationship has multiple dimensions. The United States is one of Argentina's main trading partners, but it also represents a potential source of funding for key projects and significant support for the government's economic policies.

However, not all agreements are in the same situation: some have already been signed, others still have steps to complete before taking effect, and several investment projects depend on specific negotiations and approvals.

In this context, the midterm legislative elections are a key moment for the Trump administration as they will determine the composition of Congress and its maneuverability to advance its administration, and the outcome also matters for Argentina.

Bilateral Trade

The United States is the second-largest destination for Argentine exports, accounting for 10.1% of the total, according to the latest data from INDEC.

Exports to this market experienced a year-on-year growth of 38.9%, primarily driven by industrial manufactured goods. Among the main exported products, crude oil and gold for non-monetary use dominated, accounting for 47.9% of shipments.

On the other side, the United States accounted for 9.2% of Argentina's total imports, following China and Brazil, which made up 23.3% and 21.4%, respectively.

The data shows a commercial relationship where energy and natural resources play a significant role, although there is also an exchange of industrial and technological goods.

The Trade Agreement Awaits

One of the main new economic understandings that has marked the bilateral relationship was the signing of the Reciprocal Trade and Investment Agreement (ARTI). The agreement was announced by Milei and Trump on November 13, 2025, with its final text signed on February 5, 2026.

The ARTI aims to reduce trade barriers between Argentina and the United States and increase access to each country's products in their respective markets. Among its key points, Washington committed to eliminating reciprocal tariffs on 1,675 Argentine products and expanding the quota for beef to 100,000 tons by 2026. In exchange, Argentina will eliminate tariffs on 221 categories of U.S. products and reduce 20 others to 2%, mainly auto parts.

The agreement also includes the simplification of customs and sanitary procedures, the recognition of standards for medicines and medical devices, and commitments related to intellectual property, digital trade, and services. Additionally, it incorporates mechanisms to facilitate U.S. investments in strategic sectors such as energy, mining, and infrastructure.

However, the agreement has yet to take effect as the Argentine government has not yet sent the bill to Congress. Recently, as reported by TN, the Secretary of Production Coordination, Pablo Lavigne, stated in a meeting with Amcham business leaders that the government wants to send the initiative to the Legislative Power as soon as possible. "We want to do it as quickly as possible because the approval of the law gives us both a timetable to start working on the things we have done, and at the end of the day, it starts to drift apart," he explained.

Energy and Infrastructure

The bilateral agenda also includes strategic infrastructure projects. At the end of September, the government announced a cooperation agreement for the Andes-Atlantic corridor, which anticipates investments of approximately $7 billion.

The initiative involves sectors such as energy, mining, transportation, and telecommunications. One of the projects mentioned is Argentina LNG, the liquefied natural gas development led by YPF.

In this context, the EXIM Bank of the United States presented a financing proposal of up to $6 billion for the project.

Recently, YPF CEO Horacio Marín indicated in an interview with TN that one of the company's major milestones is the signing of the final investment decision for the LNG export project, scheduled for November 26 with its international partners, the Italian company Eni and XRG, the international investment arm of the Abu Dhabi state oil company, ADNOC.

According to figures mentioned by Marín, the project involves investments of $30 billion over the next four years. The executive also referred to a potential export value of $10 billion, with a development horizon extending from 2031 to 2050.

The plan also includes the construction of a 48-inch diameter gas pipeline and a pipeline intended to transport 100,000 barrels of liquids daily. Additionally, a plant of approximately 170 hectares will be part of the infrastructure necessary for processing resources before their export.

The $20 Billion Swap

One of the most important instruments in the economic relationship is the currency swap agreement between the Argentine Central Bank and the United States Department of the Treasury. The agreement, signed in October 2025, established a swap mechanism of up to $20 billion.

During 2025, Argentina used around $2.5 billion of that agreement and repaid the utilized funds in December of that year.

The agreement remains in effect under its original conditions, and, as clarified in his latest press conference by Central Bank President Santiago Bausili, unlike the swap with China, that with the U.S. does not operate with activated tranches. "The one with the United States works differently; it does not have an activated tranche. We have an agreement that is in effect for $20 billion," he stated.

The currency agreement with the U.S. Treasury represents a key financial backing tool, especially at a time when investors are questioning how the government will fulfill its debt commitments next year.

On January 1, 1994, while Mexico celebrated the implementation of the North American Free Trade Agreement and the government projected the image of a nation moving toward the first world, the uprising of the Zapatista Army of National Liberation (EZLN) exposed a reality that this narrative kept on the sidelines: the historic abandonment of indigenous peoples. The rebellion in Chiapas challenged the country's economic and political model, but it also ensured that a local struggle resonated internationally. More than 30 years later, that eruption returns to the screen in "Marcos: Another World is Possible," a documentary by Diego Enrique Osorno, set to arrive on Netflix on December 2. The film recounts the history of Zapatismo through one of its most recognizable figures, Subcomandante Marcos, but it does not merely retrace the trajectory of a character; it seeks to understand what made that movement possible and why its questions remain relevant in a world marked by violence, authoritarianism, and inequality. After addressing the topic from a historical perspective in the series "1994" and documenting the transatlantic journey of members of the movement during the pandemic in "La Montaña," Osorno wanted to recover another dimension of that history: the emotion provoked by its public emergence. "I wanted to create something more visceral," he told MILENIO in an interview. "Something that would revive a bit of the historical emotion that I felt, and I believe millions of others felt, when the EZLN unexpectedly erupted in Chiapas, in Mexico, and in the world." The film comprises over 5,000 hours of archival footage and testimonies from photographers, journalists, soldiers, guerrillas, Zapatistas, and Marcos himself. However, Osorno's intention is not to dwell on nostalgia, but to engage with the present. He aims to provoke "political imagination," a capability he believes has been overshadowed by "too much cynicism" and "too much resignation," attitudes that limit the prospect of envisioning a different future. For this reason, the filmmaker clarifies that "the film is not hopeful, but it goes against resignation." This perspective on the present becomes significant when the documentary integrates images that transcend the history of Chiapas: the attacks of September 11, the war in Gaza, and various humanitarian crises. The question is unavoidable: what relationship exists between the critiques that Zapatismo articulated in the 1990s and the expressions of violence, dispossession, and inequality that continue to characterize the world order? Osorno acknowledges that this connection took on greater dimensions for him during the film's development. "Zapatismo 30 years ago already contained many timely issues in its discourse: climate change, feminism, structural racism—not just cultural, but structural racism, anti-globalization struggles, and struggles around the world. Zapatismo is curious; it is a movement that exists in thousands of communities in Chiapas that today maintain this autonomy and engage with the world. Contrary to how it is often attempted to be pigeonholed, Zapatismo is not in partisan political discussions in Mexico, in the nation-state," he explained. "Zapatismo is a movement that is constantly questioning things about the world. It is not dogmatic. Zapatismo is constantly asking what we do in the world, how to confront this system, how to address these cultures, how to face these autocracies, and I identify with that. As a chronicler, as a journalist, as a documentary filmmaker, I also constantly have these questions. It became very organic; I realized that toward the end of the film," he added about how he incorporated these themes.

Creating the documentary involved revisiting images that had shaped the public memory of the movement while also reconstructing an experience he had followed from a distance. "I arrived in Chiapas for the first time in 2003; I did not live through the previous part," he recalled during the conversation. At that time, he had followed Zapatismo through the internet, the press, television, and independent documentaries. Thus, reviewing records from 1994 to 2003 meant approaching a period that challenged him in every way. . . This process "was like reconstructing a bit of the emotion that I had based on the images from all these diverse records." The archive does not function solely as historical memory. Osorno sought to have the viewer experience events from a perspective different from mere retrospection. "It is a document that is historiographical in its formal approach but in its attitude is very present, in that it directly confronts the viewer rather than leading them to retrospection," he explained.

Osorno's relationship with this history also has a personal origin. When the EZLN emerged, he was 13 years old, living in Monterrey, and he remembers reading Marcos's communiqués. "I was fascinated by his prose; I was also moved by the causes he championed as the spokesperson for the movement." His arrival in Chiapas in 2003 transformed that initial fascination: "When I arrived in Chiapas, I saw what was behind the ski mask or behind the window." This experience also altered his way of seeing the character. . . For the filmmaker, Marcos cannot be understood separately from the movement that made him visible. "He is a character that matters for what he is capable of bringing to the scene, not for being a character," he explained. Therefore, the documentary does not exhaust itself in the figure of the subcommander or in his public dimension; it seeks to show what exists beyond him, the communities and collectives capable of constructing a political experience that engages with the world. The character serves as an entry point into a story that does not belong to a single man. . . Osorno also establishes the limits from which he builds this narrative. "It is not the official documentary of Marcos or the EZLN; it is my attempt to revive that emotion," he stated, as he does not intend to speak on behalf of the movement; he offers an interpretation stemming from his own relationship with Zapatismo and the questions it continues to raise for him. . . On January 1, 1994, while Mexico celebrated the implementation of the North American Free Trade Agreement and the government projected the image of a nation moving toward the first world, the uprising of the Zapatista Army of National Liberation (EZLN) exposed a reality that this narrative kept on the sidelines: the historic abandonment of indigenous peoples. The rebellion in Chiapas challenged the country's economic and political model, but it also ensured that a local struggle resonated internationally. More than 30 years later, that eruption returns to the screen in "Marcos: Another World is Possible," a documentary by Diego Enrique Osorno, set to arrive on Netflix on December 2. The film recounts the history of Zapatismo through one of its most recognizable figures, Subcomandante Marcos, but it does not merely retrace the trajectory of a character; it seeks to understand what made that movement possible and why its questions remain relevant in a world marked by violence, authoritarianism, and inequality. After addressing the topic from a historical perspective in the series "1994" and documenting the transatlantic journey of members of the movement during the pandemic in "La Montaña," Osorno wanted to recover another dimension of that history: the emotion provoked by its public emergence. "I wanted to create something more visceral," he told MILENIO in an interview. "Something that would revive a bit of the historical emotion that I felt, and I believe millions of others felt, when the EZLN unexpectedly erupted in Chiapas, in Mexico, and in the world." The film comprises over 5,000 hours of archival footage and testimonies from photographers, journalists, soldiers, guerrillas, Zapatistas, and Marcos himself. However, Osorno's intention is not to dwell on nostalgia, but to engage with the present. He aims to provoke "political imagination," a capability he believes has been overshadowed by "too much cynicism" and "too much resignation," attitudes that limit the prospect of envisioning a different future. For this reason, the filmmaker clarifies that "the film is not hopeful, but it goes against resignation." This perspective on the present becomes significant when the documentary integrates images that transcend the history of Chiapas: the attacks of September 11, the war in Gaza, and various humanitarian crises. The question is unavoidable: what relationship exists between the critiques that Zapatismo articulated in the 1990s and the expressions of violence, dispossession, and inequality that continue to characterize the world order? Osorno acknowledges that this connection took on greater dimensions for him during the film's development. "Zapatismo 30 years ago already contained many timely issues in its discourse: climate change, feminism, structural racism—not just cultural, but structural racism, anti-globalization struggles, and struggles around the world. Zapatismo is curious; it is a movement that exists in thousands of communities in Chiapas that today maintain this autonomy and engage with the world. Contrary to how it is often attempted to be pigeonholed, Zapatismo is not in partisan political discussions in Mexico, in the nation-state," he explained. "Zapatismo is a movement that is constantly questioning things about the world. It is not dogmatic. Zapatismo is constantly asking what we do in the world, how to confront this system, how to address these cultures, how to face these autocracies, and I identify with that. As a chronicler, as a journalist, as a documentary filmmaker, I also constantly have these questions. It became very organic; I realized that toward the end of the film," he added about how he incorporated these themes.

Creating the documentary involved revisiting images that had shaped the public memory of the movement while also reconstructing an experience he had followed from a distance. "I arrived in Chiapas for the first time in 2003; I did not live through the previous part," he recalled during the conversation. At that time, he had followed Zapatismo through the internet, the press, television, and independent documentaries. Thus, reviewing records from 1994 to 2003 meant approaching a period that challenged him in every way. . . This process "was like reconstructing a bit of the emotion that I had based on the images from all these diverse records." The archive does not function solely as historical memory. Osorno sought to have the viewer experience events from a perspective different from mere retrospection. "It is a document that is historiographical in its formal approach but in its attitude is very present, in that it directly confronts the viewer rather than leading them to retrospection," he explained.

Osorno's relationship with this history also has a personal origin. When the EZLN emerged, he was 13 years old, living in Monterrey, and he remembers reading Marcos's communiqués. "I was fascinated by his prose; I was also moved by the causes he championed as the spokesperson for the movement." His arrival in Chiapas in 2003 transformed that initial fascination: "When I arrived in Chiapas, I saw what was behind the ski mask or behind the window." This experience also altered his way of seeing the character. . . For the filmmaker, Marcos cannot be understood separately from the movement that made him visible. "He is a character that matters for what he is capable of bringing to the scene, not for being a character," he explained. Therefore, the documentary does not exhaust itself in the figure of the subcommander or in his public dimension; it seeks to show what exists beyond him, the communities and collectives capable of constructing a political experience that engages with the world. The character serves as an entry point into a story that does not belong to a single man. . . Osorno also establishes the limits from which he builds this narrative. "It is not the official documentary of Marcos or the EZLN; it is my attempt to revive that emotion," he stated, as he does not intend to speak on behalf of the movement; he offers an interpretation stemming from his own relationship with Zapatismo and the questions it continues to raise for him. . . When asked whether he believes this chapter has come to an end, he replied, "I don't know," and he recovers a Zapatista expression to leave that possibility open: "There is always something missing." More than providing a definitive answer regarding the current standing of Zapatismo, the documentary revisits its emergence to examine what questions remain unresolved. In that distance between what occurred in 1994 and what is yet to be imagined lies its wager: to view history not as a concluded episode but as an experience through which to interrogate the present and envision other possible futures. And today, Mexico cannot be fully understood without this part of history.

As the blue wave expanded across the United States, political and business leaders viewed the election results as a blow to President Donald Trump and his movement. Bernie Sanders, the Democratic senator, celebrated the Democrats' victory over Republicans in Congress. "The Democrats will now control the House of Representatives and the Senate and will be able to hold Trump accountable. That's great. In a time of enormous income and wealth inequality, we must do more. We must fight aggressively for working families. No more excuses," he wrote on X.

Senator Jon Ossoff, who was reelected in Georgia, interpreted the outcome as a rejection of Trump. Similarly, Democratic Representative Chris Pappas in New Hampshire described the vote as a "wake-up call" to the federal government and to lawmakers who supported cuts to healthcare and tariffs. In Texas, Republican Governor Greg Abbott acknowledged his defeat to Gina Hinojosa.

In Mexico, Larry Rubin, president of the American Society of Mexico (Amsoc), estimated that the three nations involved in the USMCA (T-MEC) will reach an agreement before the end of the year, regardless of the new composition of Congress. During the Election Night organized by Amsoc, he explained that a Democratic majority might complicate the passage of Trump's budget and bills, and anticipated short-term economic fluctuations following the election results.

Meanwhile, the Confederation of Associations of Customs Agents of the Mexican Republic (Caaarem) emphasized that it will continue to work to maintain the flow of goods and ensure operational certainty for the sector, regardless of the electoral outcome. "Mexico is the primary trading partner of the United States in goods. That relationship goes beyond an election, and we must continue to strengthen it through dialogue and institutional coordination," the organization stated. The confederation acknowledged that political changes might present new challenges but affirmed that customs agents will continue to facilitate the exchange of goods.

Earlier, in her morning press conference, President Claudia Sheinbaum highlighted that she will respect the results of the U.S. midterm elections. "We do not express opinions; it is not our place (...); we will wait for the election results and respect them, whatever they may be. We will continue on our path," she emphasized.

During the first nine months of the year, revenues for La Comer, Walmart de México, Soriana, and Chedraui grew by 0.4 percent year-on-year, increasing from 1,113.8 million to 1,118.1 million pesos compared to the same period in 2025.

According to the financial information from these companies, this stagnation is attributed to inflationary pressures, higher operating costs, consumer caution, and intense competition.

In the case of Walmart de México y Centroamérica, during the first nine months of the year, it recorded a 2.2 percent increase in revenues and a 0.2 percent rise in operating income, although its net profit fell by 2 percent year-on-year.

During a conference with analysts, Cristian Barrientos, the company's CEO, admitted that consumers are "becoming more cautious," a situation worsened by rising operational costs stemming from increases in the minimum wage and labor reform.

The executive expressed confidence in planned projects aimed at mitigating costs without compromising the value proposition, such as the "Pesos Que No Se Tocan" campaign, which includes over 4,000 items at fixed prices for more than 90 days.

Camilo Canedo, the multinational's CFO, explained that logistical optimization aims to reduce labor burdens while merging commercial growth with tight control of overall expenses.

"Customers in the Valley of Mexico are splitting their baskets to find the best alternatives in response to spending pressures," he indicated.

Regarding Soriana, during the first nine months of the year, the company experienced a 4 percent drop in revenues and a 3.3 percent decline in operating income, but achieved an 18 percent increase in profits. Toward the end of the year, the chain announced that its strategy will focus on capturing greater market share and controlling expenses.

"Consumption in Mexico has been very challenging this quarter (...) Despite the moderation of inflation, consumers remain under financial pressure and are proceeding to manage their spending very carefully, remaining highly focused on prices," stated Rodrigo Benet Córdova, the firm's CFO, during a conference call with analysts.

He added that the corporate improved its waste management and expanded its private label offerings with over 300 new SKUs in 33 categories. By the end of the year, management ruled out branch closures, limiting itself to converting two stores to the Sodimac format.

"As we move into the fourth quarter, we expect consumer spending patterns to remain very cautious. However, key seasonal events such as Buen Fin and the holiday season could present significant opportunities to improve our performance," concluded Benet Córdova, also warning about the negative impacts the upcoming tax reform could have.

Meanwhile, in the accumulated results for the first nine months of the year, La Comer continued its revenue expansion trend with sales totaling 37,300.42 million pesos, a figure that represents a 6.2 percent annual increase. However, its profits fell by 12 percent, finishing at 1,920.94 million pesos, with an accumulated earnings per share.

During a conference with analysts, Héctor de la Barreda, the company's CEO, highlighted that the dynamism in its sales allowed it to surpass the indicator from the National Association of Self-Service and Department Stores (ANTAD) by nearly 300 basis points.

Looking ahead, the retailer's management acknowledged facing a "slow consumption environment" and ruled out immediate expansion plans for its pilot format City Market Cafe, focusing instead on strengthening its loyalty program, sustaining seasonal promotional campaigns like Temporada Naranja, and capitalizing on the double-digit growth they are experiencing in their digital channels.

Finally, during the first nine months of the year, Grupo Chedraui reported declines of 4 percent in revenues, 2.1 percent in operating income, and 5 percent in net profit; however, it slightly exceeded expectations in the penultimate quarter.

According to a stock report published by Barclays, the company boosted efficiencies in its distribution centers, consolidated better terms with suppliers in the U.S., and executed more effective promotions nationwide.

The analysis by the financial institution considered that the opening of 26 new branches in Mexico favored total billing and supported Chedraui's margin stability. While its Smart & Final format remained stable in the United States, the chains targeting the Hispanic market, El Super and Fiesta Mart, felt the effects of macroeconomic shocks, prompting Barclays specialists to project that any further improvements will depend directly on the stabilization of customer traffic in those stores.

Adds detail from minutes report

SANTIAGO, Nov 4 (Reuters) - Policymakers at Chile's central bank considered keeping the rate unchanged or increasing it by 25 basis points as "plausible" options at its last meeting, minutes showed on Wednesday.

The bank's board unanimously decided to hold borrowing costs at 4.5% at the meeting last week.

• All board members agreed about the importance of continuing to analyze the evolution of the economy for future decisions and pointed to a particularly challenging current macroeconomic scenario

• "Until now, the cost shock had been proving more persistent than anticipated, but its impact had been limited, largely due to weak domestic demand," the minutes said

• Policymakers concurred that the rise in cost pressures observed since the previous meeting had increased the risk that the economic shocks accumulated since March, such as oil, would propagate to other prices with greater force

• Various board members stated that Chile should be prepared for a more restrictive monetary policy scenario

(Reporting by Aida Pelaez-Fernandez and Natalia Ramos; Editing by Andrew Heavens, William Maclean)

SECTION 6 CORPORATE PROFILE

6.1 Activities

Fomento Económico Mexicana S.A.B. de C.V. (FEMSA), a Monterrey, Mexico-based multinational conglomerate, is primarily engaged in the production, bottling, and distribution of beverages through its Coca-Cola FEMSA subsidiary, which operates as one of the world's largest Coca-Cola franchisees. The company also manages a vast retail network, including the OXXO convenience store chain, which dominates Mexico's retail landscape and extends into select international markets. Additionally, FEMSA operates in logistics, fuel retailing, and health sciences. The fastest-growing segments include retail, driven by the aggressive expansion of OXXO stores and digital initiatives that enhance customer convenience, as well as beverage operations in emerging markets, fueled by rising consumer demand for non-alcoholic drinks and strategic acquisitions. This diversified approach has positioned FEMSA as a resilient player in the global consumer goods sector, emphasizing innovation and sustainability. It is the International Depository Receipt (IDR) market's 5th largest Beverages company by market capitalization.

SECTION 6 CORPORATE PROFILE

6.1 Activities

America Movil S.A.B. de C.V., a leading telecommunications provider headquartered in Mexico, operates across Latin America, including Mexico, Central and South America, and the Caribbean. The company specializes in mobile and fixed-line telephony, broadband internet, pay television, and related digital services, serving over 280 million customers through its extensive network infrastructure. Its core business revolves around delivering wireless communication, high-speed data connectivity, and entertainment solutions, with a strong emphasis on innovation in 5G technology and fiber-optic expansions. The fastest-growing segments include mobile data services, driven by rising smartphone adoption and demand for streaming content, as well as broadband offerings through fiber-to-the-home deployments, which have seen significant expansion in urban and emerging markets. This strategic focus has positioned America Movil as a key player in bridging the digital divide, fostering economic growth in the regions it serves. It is the International Depository Receipt (IDR) market's 3rd largest Telecommunication company by market capitalization.

SECTION 6 CORPORATE PROFILE

6.1 Activities

Grupo Aeroportuario del Sureste S.A. de C.V. (ASUR) is a prominent Mexican airport operator, managing a portfolio of 10 airports in the southeastern region, including the high-traffic Cancun International Airport. Its core business involves the operation, maintenance, and development of airport infrastructure, encompassing passenger and cargo handling, commercial concessions, and ancillary services like retail and parking. ASUR focuses on enhancing efficiency and passenger experience to support growing aviation demand. The company's fastest-growing segments include international passenger traffic, fueled by tourism in destinations such as Cancun and the Riviera Maya, as well as non-aeronautical revenues from expanded retail and food services, which have seen robust increases due to rising traveler spending and airport expansions. This strategic emphasis has solidified ASUR's role in Mexico's aviation industry, contributing to economic connectivity and regional development. It is the International Depository Receipt (IDR) market's 12th largest Airlines company by market capitalization.

Grupo Aeroportuario del Sureste SAB de CV is the trade name used on the Mexico Stock Exchange and Grupo Aeroportuario del Sureste S.A. de C.V. is used on the New York Stock Exchange.

6.1 Activities

Grupo Aeroportuario del Sureste S.A. de C.V. (ASUR) is a prominent Mexican airport operator, managing a portfolio of 10 airports in the southeastern region, including the high-traffic Cancun International Airport. Its core business involves the operation, maintenance, and development of airport infrastructure, encompassing passenger and cargo handling, commercial concessions, and ancillary services like retail and parking. ASUR focuses on enhancing efficiency and passenger experience to support growing aviation demand. The company's fastest-growing segments include international passenger traffic, fueled by tourism in destinations such as Cancun and the Riviera Maya, as well as non-aeronautical revenues from expanded retail and food services, which have seen robust increases due to rising traveler spending and airport expansions. This strategic emphasis has solidified ASUR's role in Mexico's aviation industry, contributing to economic connectivity and regional development. It is the International Depository Receipt (IDR) market's 12th largest Airlines company by market capitalization.

Grupo Aeroportuario del Sureste SAB de CV is the trade name used on the Mexico Stock Exchange and Grupo Aeroportuario del Sureste S.A. de C.V. is used on the New York Stock Exchange.

6.1 Activities

Grupo Aeroportuario del Pacifico S.A.B. de C.V. (GAP) is a prominent Mexican airport operator, managing a network of 12 airports primarily in the Pacific region, including key hubs like Guadalajara and Puerto Vallarta. Its core business centers on the operation, maintenance, and development of these facilities, encompassing passenger and cargo handling, aeronautical services, and non-aeronautical revenue streams such as retail, advertising, and parking. GAP has seen robust growth in passenger traffic, with international routes emerging as the fastest-growing segment, fueled by rising tourism and business travel demands. Additionally, cargo operations and commercial activities, particularly e-commerce-related logistics, have expanded rapidly, contributing to overall revenue diversification. This strategic focus on infrastructure upgrades and efficiency enhancements positions GAP as a key player in Mexico's aviation sector, supporting economic connectivity and sustainable growth. It is the International Depository Receipt (IDR) market's 4th largest Engineering & construction company by market capitalization.

Operating under a concession model, ASUR focuses on efficiency and sustainability to capitalize on Mexico's rising air travel demand, positioning the company as a vital player in the country's aviation sector. Grupo Aeroportuario del Centro Norte, S.A.B. de C.V. (OMA) is a prominent Mexican airport operator, managing a network of 13 airports primarily in the north-central region, including key hubs like Monterrey. Its core business activities focus on the operation, maintenance, and development of airport infrastructure, encompassing passenger handling, cargo services, commercial concessions, and real estate development. The company generates revenue through aeronautical fees, such as landing and parking charges, as well as non-aeronautical sources like retail, advertising, and parking. 5.1 Activities

Kimberly-Clark de Mexico S.A.B. de C.V., a leading subsidiary of the global Kimberly-Clark Corporation, operates primarily in Mexico, focusing on the manufacture, marketing, and distribution of personal care and consumer tissue products. The company's core activities encompass a wide range of essential items, including diapers, wipes, feminine hygiene products, and household tissues under well-known brands like Huggies, Kleenex, and Scott. These offerings address everyday hygiene and health needs, emphasizing quality, innovation, and sustainability. In recent years, the fastest-growing segments have been baby and child care products, fueled by rising consumer demand for premium, eco-friendly options, and adult incontinence solutions, driven by an aging population and increased health awareness. Additionally, the company has seen strong expansion in feminine care, supported by targeted marketing and product diversification, positioning it as a key player in Mexico's consumer goods market. It is Mexico's largest Forest products & paper company by market capitalization.

4.1 Activities

Corp Inmobiliaria Vesta SAB de CV is a leading industrial real estate developer based in Mexico, specializing in the acquisition, development, leasing, and management of high-quality industrial properties such as warehouses, distribution centers, and logistics facilities. The company's core activities focus on serving manufacturing, e-commerce, and logistics sectors, primarily in strategic locations across Mexico to capitalize on nearshoring trends and cross-border trade. In recent years, Vesta's fastest-growing segments have been modern logistics and e-commerce fulfillment centers, driven by the surge in online retail and manufacturing relocation from Asia to Mexico. This expansion has strengthened Vesta's portfolio, positioning it as a key contributor to Mexico's industrial infrastructure, with a commitment to sustainable practices and tenant-focused services that enhance operational efficiency and long-term value. It is Mexico's largest Real estate company by market capitalization.

NYSE STOCK REPORT

PHOENIX, Tuesday, November 03 2026 - Ahead of this morning's market opening, Southern Copper Corporation closed lower the previous trading day. Southern Copper Corporation (NYSE:SCCO), the NYSE's largest Non ferrous metals sector company by market cap, fell 2.2% during its previous trading session to close at $173.49.

Southern Copper Corporation (NYSE:SCCO) is a leading integrated copper producer, renowned for its extensive copper mining operations and low-cost production capabilities. Core activities encompass large-scale copper mining, smelting, and refining through key assets like the Toquepala and Cuajone mines, alongside Mexico's strategic copper operations. The company excels in producing copper concentrates and cathodes, while also generating molybdenum and silver byproducts. Southern Copper sustains its competitive edge through significant copper reserves, supporting industrial copper supply and expansion projects. Emphasizing sustainability, the company adopts innovative mining practices and maintains robust supply chain management, positioning itself to leverage long-term trends in electric vehicles and base metals demand.

SANTIAGO, 4 nov (Reuters) - Los consejeros del Banco Central de Chile estuvieron de acuerdo en la última reunión de política monetaria, de fines de octubre, en que era plausible evaluar tanto mantener la tasa en 4,5% como aumentarla en 25 puntos base, aunque primó la primera opción, según las minutas del encuentro publicadas el miércoles.

Los consejeros coincidieron en que la evolución esperada de la economía era importante para el análisis de ajustes a la tasa, que está en 4,5% desde diciembre pasado.

"Todos los Consejeros coincidieron en que el alza de las presiones de costos observada desde la Reunión anterior había elevado el riesgo de que el shock acumulado desde marzo terminara propagándose hacia otros precios con mayor fuerza y adquiriera una persistencia mayor que la habitual", señalaron las minutas.

Debido a lo anterior, hubo acuerdo entre los consejeros que se trataba de un escenario complejo ya que una vez que las expectativas y los mecanismos de formación de precios comenzaban a desajustarse, "el costo de restablecer la convergencia podía ser considerablemente mayor".

"En ese contexto, todos los Consejeros estuvieron de acuerdo en que era plausible evaluar tanto la opción de mantener la TPM en 4,5% como la de aumentarla en 25 puntos base (pb), hasta 4,75%", dijo la nota.

Por eso, la evolución de la economía era importante para este análisis, señalaron los consejeros. Por un lado, la debilidad de la demanda podía ser más persistente y generar holguras de capacidad para contener las presiones inflacionarias.

Por otro, varios consejeros dijeron que "no existían antecedentes suficientes para pensar que no se daría la recuperación prevista de la demanda y que, en ese escenario, las presiones inflacionarias de mediano plazo serían mayores que las proyectadas" en el reporte de política monetaria de septiembre.

"Y se debía estar preparado para un escenario más restrictivo para la política monetaria", añadieron.

(Reporte de Natalia Ramos y Aida Peláez Fernández
)

((Mesa de edición en español, santiago.desk@thomsonreuters.com ))

"En ese contexto, todos los Consejeros estuvieron de acuerdo en que era plausible evaluar tanto la opción de mantener la TPM en 4,5% como la de aumentarla en 25 puntos base (pb), hasta 4,75%", dijo la nota.

Por eso, la evolución de la economía era importante para este análisis, señalaron los consejeros. Por un lado, la debilidad de la demanda podía ser más persistente y generar holguras de capacidad para contener las presiones inflacionarias.

Por otro, varios consejeros dijeron que "no existían antecedentes suficientes para pensar que no se daría la recuperación prevista de la demanda y que, en ese escenario, las presiones inflacionarias de mediano plazo serían mayores que las proyectadas" en el reporte de política monetaria de septiembre.

"Y se debía estar preparado para un escenario más restrictivo para la política monetaria", añadieron.

(Reporte de Natalia Ramos y Aida Peláez Fernández
)

Madrid, November 4 (EFE) - Workers from Colombia and Venezuela lead the registrations in the Spanish Social Security related to the extraordinary regularization process for immigrants that began in April.

According to data collected until the end of October, the number of employment registrations for foreigners reached 490,586. Of this total, 27.6% were Colombians and 15.7% were Venezuelans, as detailed by the Social Security office on Thursday.

Out of all immigrant workers, 75.2% are enrolled in the general Social Security scheme, while 5.9% are self-employed. By gender, 59.7% are men and 40.3% are women.

In October, the dynamism of foreign employment continued, bolstered by the extraordinary regularization process of immigrants, with an additional 63,899 registered, bringing the total close to 3.7 million in the Social Security system.

The Spanish labor market set a new record in October, reaching 22.62 million employed individuals after adding an average of 186,612 registrations to the Social Security, marking the largest increase for this month in historical data, largely due to the education sector.

Regarding unemployment, it increased by 43,128 people, totaling 2.42 million, representing the largest rise in October since the pandemic, "in a context of high labor market participation," according to data published today by the ministries of Labor and Social Security.

In terms of annual comparison from October to October, unemployment decreased by 21,133 individuals (0.86% less), while employment increased by 784,573, reflecting an annual growth rate of 3.6%.

In the sector data, the largest increase in registrations for October was in education, with 165,994 more, coinciding with the start of the academic year, while the sharpest decline occurred in hospitality, with 44,974 fewer employed following the significant summer tourism campaign.

By gender, job growth was higher among women, with 131,934 additional registrations, surpassing 10.7 million. Among men, registrations increased by 54,678, reaching 11.9 million.

Women now represent 47.4% of the total registered workers.

Regarding self-employed workers, there was an increase of 17,963 in October, exceeding 3.5 million for the first time, and an annual increase of 79,163.

Conversely, the number of unemployed people grew among those from the services sector (26,853 more), but also in industry (1,911 more) and agriculture (1,547 more), while the construction sector saw little change (102 more). EFE

A little more than a decade ago, Donald Trump began his journey to the White House with a racist warning that Mexico was sending to the United States "rapists," "criminals," and "the worst" of its people. Eleven years later, the American political landscape sent him a very different message: a historic defeat driven largely by the Latino vote and the rise of politicians of Mexican descent and other minority groups that reconfigured the balance of power in Washington.

The 2026 midterm elections in the northern neighbor undoubtedly dealt one of the most severe political blows to the U.S. president, who, far from claiming fraud, as he did six years ago with Joe Biden's victory, had to resign himself to acknowledging the bitter reality of adversity in the face of the blue tsunami, under the pretext that if he had appeared on the ballot, the story would have been different.

The Democrats regained control of the Senate, moved closer to a majority in the House of Representatives, and secured several key positions thanks to a decisive turnout from the Hispanic electorate, particularly from citizens of Mexican descent.

Among the most notable victories were the election of Gina Hinojosa as Texas' first Latina governor, the victory of Texan singer Bobby Pulido in an important House district, and the triumph of Xavier Becerra in California's executive branch. All three... of Mexican descent. Thus, the victory of three compatriots.

The Latino vote takes its toll on Trump... but was this already anticipated?

Although Donald Trump made gains among some Hispanic groups in 2024, the 2026 elections showed a turnaround that ultimately impacted the Old Grand Party (GOP) that nominated him in 2016 and two years ago.

However, prior polls already indicated that the Democrats maintained a 27-point advantage among Latino voters for the congressional elections, and more than half of this electorate viewed their vote as a way to curb the Republican president.

In addition, Trump's approval rating among Hispanics, one of the demographic groups most affected by Republican policies, significantly declined during his second term, according to the Pew Research Center.

In Texas, the local outlet The Texas Tribune emphasized that the Latino electorate leaned once again toward Democratic candidates, motivated by concerns about the cost of living, the economy, and corruption.

Gina Hinojosa makes history in Texas: She will be the first governor of Mexican descent

One of the biggest political blows to the Republicans occurred in Texas, a historical stronghold of the elephant party.

After decades of GOP dominance, Democrat Gina Hinojosa, of Mexican descent, defeated Governor Greg Abbott, who had run with a strong anti-Mexican rhetoric, and became the first Latina woman to govern the state, breaking a streak of more than thirty years without a Democratic governor in the entity.

Her campaign focused on combating the high cost of living, corruption, and access to economic opportunities.

Bobby Pulido reshapes the political landscape of South Texas

Regional music performer Bobby Pulido also achieved one of the anticipated results of election day by defeating, if not overwhelming, Republican Monica De La Cruz in Texas' 15th District.

During the campaign, Pulido, who was insulted by Trump during the early hours of election day, sought to connect particularly with Hispanic voters through a message focused on family economics, wealth creation, and support for the communities of the Rio Grande Valley.

Now, Trump will have no choice but to sing at night: "I'm losing sleep."

Xavier Becerra wins in California

In California, Xavier Becerra, of Mexican descent, won the gubernatorial election, consolidating another significant win for the Democrats, whose outgoing governor, Gavin Newsom, is seen as a potential successor to Trump in the Oval Office.

Additionally, Becerra made history by becoming the first Latino governor of California, where Los Angeles, the state's most populous city, houses the largest Mexican-origin community in the world outside of Mexico City, surpassing cities like Monterrey and Guadalajara.

The former Secretary of Health of the United States and former Attorney General of California reaffirmed Democratic dominance in the state with a campaign focused on health, housing, and economy, keeping California as one of the party's main strongholds, according to The Washington Post.

Abdul El-Sayed makes history: He will be the first Muslim senator in the United States

Another historical victory of the day occurred in Michigan, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, another thorn in Trump's side, was elected to the federal Senate, becoming the first Muslim to arrive in the United States Senate.

El-Sayed, a physician and former public health director of Detroit, kept the seat in Democratic hands after a campaign in which he was constantly targeted by the U.S. president, who, with racist overtones, questioned his religion and political views.

His victory was celebrated by progressive and civil rights organizations as a step forward in minority representation within the U.S. Congress.

Historic setback for Donald Trump

This national result represents the greatest political setback for Donald Trump since his return to the White House.

The Democrats regained the Senate after winning historically Republican states like Texas, Kansas, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Ohio, while solidifying a majority in the House of Representatives.

In addition to inflation, the cost of living, gas prices, and various controversies surrounding the Republican administration, such as ICE's crackdown and the war in Iran, ultimately dealt Trump a heavy blow at the polls.

After the Republican defeat was confirmed, Trump asserted that he is "absolutely willing to accept" the election results and stated that he would seek to work with Democrats over the next two years.

However, he also maintained that had he appeared on the ballot, the Republicans would have won "by a landslide," while warning that he would use his veto power to block initiatives from the donkey party with which he disagrees.
